I'm talking about the evangelical church in general now, not just the Reformed church. The church in general... has really not got a very good grip on the concept that every believer is a prophet, a priest, and a king. Frank Tillepaw, who has written a book, The Unleashing of the Church, though I think in one edition it's called The Church Unleashed, maybe the more modern edition or the later edition it's called Unleashing the Church, whatever, He has a set of tapes that will be awfully intriguing for you to get. And he, in there, tells a couple of reasons why the church as it is today is in a situation where there is a passive laity and where outreach to the world is also... truncated. He talks about the making of a fortress church. A fortress church to him means a church that stays in, does not reach out, and it also means a church in which the laity are passive. And he has a couple of pretty interesting principles, well not principles, a couple of explanations. for why the church got to be the way it is and what to do about it. And I put these things down in terms of four statements. They're the sort of common sorts of statements you might hear people say. The first statement is, it's the they can come to us statement. Tillapa believes and says that part of the passive laity is because of the... what he calls the parachurch explosion. Since World War II in this country, a terrific amount of outreach ministry has gone on through parachurch ministries. Now, by the way, Dilipat is not being negative about parachurch. Let me tell you what he says. He says he was a navigator, and I would never have been a navigator, so I may be not recounting his history as well as I should. to Dawson Trotman, who was trying to reach young sailors, when he tried to get churches to reach out to the sailors in town, the typical response was, well, we have a singles group, or we have a college and career group. Let them come to us. And what Trotman decided was that if you're going to go to people, rather than say, let them come to us, you're going to have to do an end run around the local church. Because the local church was stuck in a position where it said, we have our groups. We have our men's group and our women's group. We have our youth group and our college and career group and so on. If people want to, if you're going to reach people, let them come to us. Our doors are open to everybody. And Trotman decided, my word, if I'm going to really reach people, I'm going to have to do an end run around the church. So what he has done... was he started the Navigators, which was a parachurch ministry, a specialized ministry that went out to the people who were sailors, the people who were in the military, went to them and found them and grabbed them and won them. Now, Telepah says when you ask the typical church, when you ask anybody, what does the church do? When you think of a local church, what does it do? You think of six or eight things. Think of worship.and preaching. You think of the ministry of music. You think of Sunday school. You think of men's groups, women's groups, children's ministries, youth groups. But as Tillapa says, when you think of the church, you don't think of jail ministries. You don't think of ministries to unwed mothers. You don't think of ministries to the military. You don't think of ministries to international students. You don't think of all these kinds of ministries. Basically, if you're not white, upper-middle-class family, you don't think of all these kinds of ministries. Basically, if you're not white, upper-middle-class family, There's not much place for you in the church. And almost anyone who has wanted to reach for Christ, any group in this country, besides a white upper middle class family group, has almost had to go do an end run around the evangelical church and form some kind of parent church ministry that actually reaches college students, or actually reaches high school dropouts, or who reaches prisoners, or who, you see what I'm saying. They had to become parachurch ministries. The thing that's a little bit embarrassing is that though the parachurch ministries have always said we're an arm of the church, the parachurch ministries have become much more vital in many cases in the church, the local church. For example, and again, I know I'm being taped and so on, so I probably should have checked and double-checked all of my... all of the statements, but Frank Tillepa says that the largest missionary sending body among denominations in the world is the Southern Baptist Church, but the Campus Crusade for Christ actually has three times the number of missionaries that the Southern Baptist Church has got. And that the parachurch ministries, by and large, are far more vital than local churches. And it can be a little bit embarrassing in a sense because the parachurch ministry, the parachurch is saying we're an arm of the church, but if you consider the arm being this big and the rest of the body being this big, it does look a little bit strange. In a certain sense, parachurch ministries are the fishermen and the local church has decided we're the aquarium. And... Now, who's to blame for that? There's a certain sense in which the parachurch ministries have developed because of this mentality, but the parachurch ministries, to a certain degree, because they've had to do an in-run around the local church, have continued to contribute to that mentality. If you want to reach prostitutes, form a parachurch ministry. Why? I mean, you don't think any church is going to do that. The church won't be specialized enough. The church won't get behind it. You want to do that, you have to form your own ministry, a parachurch ministry, you see. So the let them come to us is a mentality that Telepost says that it has gone along with creating a fortress church. And that is this bifurcation between parachurch, fishermen, and the local church, which continues to be kind of an aquarium. It's unfortunate, however, that an awful lot of the people that parachurch ministries reach just don't fit in most local churches. They don't fit. They're because very often they're not families or because they're not our kind of people. And very often parachurch ministries develop their own, almost become their own kind of church for that reason. Another reason that Tilipa mentions that they're part of the making of the fortress church, we must have our needs met. Now, Tilipa calls this class captivity. Let me briefly explain what he says here. After World War II, again, we're talking about America, in this country, We had a problem. America, in order to win World War II, had taken all of its vast resources, and we have a lot of resources here, and we had developed an incredible manufacturing capacity. In order to win the war, we were just producing planes and bombs and tanks and producing... manufactured goods at a rate that the world had never seen before, that no country had ever been able to muster that kind of manufacturing capacity. Suddenly, as soon as we had no war, we had a problem. The whole economy was based on manufacturing, so we had to do something. And what actually happened was, in the late 40s and early 50s, we had a phenomenon called advertising. The advertising industry convinced Americans that they needed an awful lot of goods in order to make us incredible consumers, the greatest consumers in the world, so that we could keep this incredible manufacturing machine alive and so that the economy could continue to progress. And they did it. There's no group of people in the world that believes that they need more goods than Americans. And because American middle class people are so consumer oriented, above all, we love inventory. We like to pick and to choose. We're highly, highly, highly, highly aware of our needs. As a result, middle class churches have become commissaries. The churches is, this is Telepaw's idea. It uses that term, commissary. that the evangelical church, by and large, is captive to the middle class and to the agenda of the middle class. What I mean by that is, number one, it means that the middle class says to the churches, if you meet our needs, if you have enough choirs and handbell choirs, if you have enough of an inventory, enough programs that meet our needs, we'll come to you. And so the middle class church tends to orient itself toward issues of property. Middle class churches like to have nice carpeting and like to have a big wing and like to have a marble building and that sort of thing. Ministries assume that people have got the basic good quality of life. Middle class churches do not minister to people who don't have the basic safe life. They don't minister to non-middle class people. Middle-class churches would rather spend money on property than people in general, rather than pour its money into people's needs. Middle-class churches would like to have a bigger sanctuary, would like to have bigger events, bigger worship services, bigger choirs, and so forth. But in general, the middle class says, if you meet our needs... will come to you. And so churches, the evangelical church is more of a client, evangelical church people are more of a clientele than a congregation. That's what Martin Marty says. You understand the difference between a clientele and a congregation? It's very easy to grow a church as long as you study the market. I'm using the term church growth in the most nasty way. It's very easy to swell your roles. If you segment the market and you figure out what the people in this particular area want, and then you program to meet those needs, you'll have people come. Because we're so incredibly consumer-oriented. That's the reason why, by and large, you find more of the super churches in this country than you do other places in the world in many cases. Anyway, we must have our needs met. But that contributes to a fortress church, you see. The people come to get their needs met, not to pour themselves out, you see, in deeds of compassion and care and service to people around them. They come to have their needs being met. A third factor making for the fortress church, we can't work with you, is... Well, it's the controversies. You have to realize that because of the great liberal fundamentalist controversy in the country, you have a great bifurcation between the fundamentalists who feel like they have to defend the faith and the liberals who in many cases have got... a good social conscience. And one of the great difficulties we have is a big bifurcation between churches that put a lot of emphasis on teaching and emphasis on regeneration and churches that put emphasis on ministry and service to people. And frankly, in a church where the theology is universalistic and where the preaching cannot possibly create regenerate people... And you need regenerate people with the power of the Spirit to really pour themselves out in deeds of ministry to people. Here you've got churches where the preaching can't produce power, where the people are being asked to do all kinds of tremendous programs pouring themselves out for people. And then here you've got churches that are just growing fat, on the other hand. with people who are learning from the Word of God and people who are growing in grace. And very often, as they get older, they're growing in their pocketbooks. But all they do when they come together is talk. They talk about this stuff. They have seminars. They have classes. All they do is talk. And because of that bifurcation and because... The way Frank Tillipoff puts it, because of all the liberal fundamentalist controversies, we're very, very suspicious of one another. And when it says we can't work with you, that refers to the kind of attitude that means if you don't toe the line, if you don't toe our doctrinal line, if you don't look like you're one of us. We can't possibly work with you. It means, for example, that pastors and officers are scared to let lay people lead unless the lay people are as thoroughly schooled in the doctrine as they are. And basically what we're telling lay people is that until you become as well-schooled in doctrine as we are, we don't want you to really take initiative. We don't want you to reach out. We don't want you to minister. You wait for us to tell you what to do. or you sign up on the bulletin board under the sheets where we have decided what ministries are to be done. And telepopulities, to a great degree, it's the denominational splits and the liberal fundamentalist controversy is a problem. Another area, where are your credentials? This refers to, and this is another factor in the making of Fortress Church, Passive Laity. I... White evangelical churches, by and large, are awfully, awfully uptight about people having the degrees, having the right credentials for things. We have a Greek model of education. The Greek model of education is totally academic. It's very different than Jesus' model. See, the way in which Jesus taught his disciples was not that he had them come to a classroom. where he lectured, but instead he picked the disciples up and he took them out into the world. And as things happened to them, Jesus would say, notice this, notice this, and he would teach as he went. He had an apprenticeship model. He had a life-on-a-life model, a discipling model. Now what's interesting is parachurch ministries, by and large, are very anti-seminary. Is that just an accident? Parachurch ministries are very vital in terms of outreach. Parachurch ministries are very anti-clerical. They don't like to have a lot of ministers around. They're run by lay people. Why is that? I think because in some ways they're more in tune with Jesus' model of letting lay people minister, of training them on the job and making sure they're being trained in wisdom as well as knowledge. You see, in a lot of ways, they are more in tune with what the Bible says about the fact that every believer is a prophet and a priest and a king. But in the fortress church, you have the attitude that really only the officers are prophets, priests, and kings. We can't trust the lay people. Or lay people are, because they're under the middle class American... They don't think of themselves as prophets, priests, and kings. They want to find the best prophet and the best priest and the best kings in town so they can go and have their needs met. They don't think of themselves as prophets, priests, and kings. That's behind the fortress church. And I think that... Boy, I think that what Tilapa is saying is something that is really, really important. He says what we have to do in order to overcome that is to press people that they are ministers, messengers, and managers, and that the lay people need to be told that, and that then they have to be shown that we do trust in the minister. One thing you might find kind of interesting is... Telepah hates committees, absolutely hates committees. In fact, I don't think he has a committee in his church. He may overdo this, but he says when he was in the army, he said whenever you're on the front line of a war, you will find that on the front line where your life is on the line, there's a lot of camaraderie, there's a lot of... cohesion to the team. The people are working with each other because, man, your life is on the line. We're buddies. We've got to work together. We've got to pull together. We've got to get the morale is often high, at least unless there's been a whole lot of horrible defeats. But you go back a couple of miles, just a couple of miles from the battle line, he would say, where you have the supply line. and the supply camps, and there's nothing but complaining and grumbling and mumbling about the food and backbiting between parties and so forth. And he says the reason that most churches are in a position where they are like the supply line camps rather than the front line camps is because we keep most lay people in rear echelon ministries. We put them on Christian ed committees and we put them on music committees and we put them on all kinds of committees instead of saying to the lay people, You should be in the jails. You should be on the college campuses. You should be in the ghetto. You should be out there ministering to people. That's front line kinds of ministry. And so he says, for example, instead of having a Christian ed committee that runs the Vacation Bible School as well as Sunday School, instead you should be saying, okay, lay people, is there anybody out there that's got a burden for ministry to children? Get together and do it. If there's nobody with a burden for a vacation Bible school this year, if there's nobody that wants to do it, nobody's got a burden on their heart to do it, we're not going to do it. If you have a Christian education committee, you've institutionalized vacation Bible school. By institutionalizing, I mean you appoint people to this Christian education committee. The person gets on there, maybe they don't even really want to get on there, but they get on there because you've pulled their leg. And they say, okay, what does the Christian education committee do? One of the things is we run vacation Bible school. Who's going to be the director this year? Well, I don't know, we're going to have to go find one. And you get up there and say, we won't even be able to have to have a Christian education, we won't be able to have a vacation Bible school this year unless somebody volunteers as a director. So you work on the congregation to get, you know, using guilt and so on. And a committee structure, Telepas says, institutionalizes and creates a rear echelon mentality. What lies behind that? those factors that we just went over. Instead, tell lay people, we are letting you minister here. We want you to minister here. You see a need, come to us and say, I want to meet that need. Get together the other people who want to meet that need. Go to it. We'll guide you, we'll help you, we'll support you. We're not going to control you. We're not necessarily going to look at your doctrine up and down before we let you even make a move. So, telepath says, this is what you have to do. Ordinarily, to be a deacon, I mean, to be a priest or become a bishop, you have to be a deacon for a period of time, so it's almost a rank on the way on up. And there is some basis for talking about this. For example, in Acts 19.22, Timothy and Erastus... are Paul's helpers. They're sent to Macedonia and Paul calls them their deacons. Right? Because the idea of a deacon was a helper. In fact, you also even have the classic text in Acts 6 that talks about the fact that here were the apostles and they had jobs that they had to delegate to somebody else. They needed to get the details of a particular job off of them so that they could devote themselves to the ministry of the word. And they ordained the seven, who obviously were in a helping capacity. And they took duties off of the apostles so that they could concentrate on the ministry of the word. And so there's a case for saying that one of the things that deacons do is to administratively assist the elders and pastors. Second historic view, okay, is the view that says deacons are trustees. And that is their financial officers, maintainers of the property. Basically, the basic gift that would be the key gift for trustees would be the gift of giving. They're basically stewards. A trustee is a steward, and their basic concern is stewardship. They bring the money in, they handle the money, they seek to develop the gift of liberality and the people, the grace of liberality, I mean. They... make that effort, and they are the financial officers and they care for all the real property of the congregation. And this basically comes to us from the Scottish Church, the Scottish Kirk. If you read the first and second books of discipline, the original charters of the Scottish Church, you'll see the deacons. By the way, those deacons in the Roman Catholic understanding do help the poor. because they take the alms the bishop gives them and they distribute them. And though in this Scottish understanding, Scottish tradition, the deacons did care for the poor, the deacons were the financial officers for the whole parish, so that they took care of the schools, they took care of disbursements to the pastors, they took care of disbursements to the poor as well. So taking care of the poor was part of their job, but not the main focus. They really were the trustees. Now, what biblical basis is there for that? I must say, in my opinion, and I have a microphone, so that's something important here. My opinion is that it's really very weak, but... It's got a very weak biblical basis, but it's still a valid inference from the good understanding of what deacons can do. In the synagogue, in the Jewish synagogues in the dispersion, there were two kinds of officers. There were the elders and there were the Kazan. And the Kazan were people who really stood pretty much in the tradition of the Levites. The Levites took care of the property of the church, of the tabernacle, and they also distributed alms to the poor. And the Kazan did the same thing. They took care of the property and they distributed alms to the poor. And a lot of people said, well, look, it's obvious that the deacons stood in the place. The deacons and elders of the New Testament church were just basically the elders and the Kazan of the synagogue. And there's some... sense in which that's true, but you see what I'm saying about it being kind of a way of stretching a point. There's no doubt that deacons are considered to be standing in the shoes of the priests, because we're told that taking care of the poor, giving alms, dealing with people's physical needs was the work of the priests in the Old Testament. And you even have a place, for example, in Hebrews 13, 15 and 16, where it's telling us that we're all priests, and we're that we all have access to the holy place through Jesus, our great high priest. And it says, don't forget to share what you have and do good, for these are pleasing sacrifices. See, it's all couched in priestly liturgical language. Deeds of mercy to the poor are a well-pleasing priestly sacrifice. And so in that sense, you can say, yes, the deacons stand in the shoes of the Levites. Yes, the Levites took care of the property. And therefore, it certainly wouldn't be a bad thing to say the deacons should do this sort of thing. But I'm not sure that it's by any means the most... I don't think by any means it's the primary purpose of the deacons. And it certainly doesn't... You can't make a case from the Bible that that's a very important thing for deacons to be doing. The third basic approach... is that deacons are ministers of mercy. Yes? Which reference? Hebrews 13, 15, and 16, right. And this is they are to care for the felt needs of people. material, economic, distress. And Romans 12, 8 talks about a gift of mercy. And in this view, that's the key. And it's from the Dutch Reformed Churches, from the Continental Churches, that we get this view. It says that the main thing deacons should be doing is taking care of people in need. The Dutch churches were mighty good at it. In 17th century Amsterdam, the deacons of the Reformed Church in Amsterdam ran an orphanage, ran several homes for the elderly, ran eight schools, a clothing manufacturing shop, and bakeries. And every Thursday, the poor of Amsterdam would come to see the deacons. The deacons would care for them, pray for them, examine their need, and on the basis of the need, they would give them tokens. The tokens were not money negotiable at any place except at the deacons' industries. So the person could take the tokens and get bread, could get food, could get clothing. And the deacons also ran a hospital. And there was committees of deacons and deaconesses that ran the hospital and the orphanage and the home for the elderly and the manufacturing shops and so on. They really were the backbone of social coherence in the town. And you will find today that this is the primary. In fact, if you go to the Christian Reformed Church, you take a look at their articles, you'll see that there is no mention under the work of the deacon. There's no mention of trusteeship at all. And there's no mention even really of helps, but it's all of mercy. Now, the American Presbyterians have been mostly influenced by which view? The middle view. Yeah, well, I mean, because we've been mostly influenced by British and therefore Scottish Presbyterianism. There has been a great deal of debate about this. Some of you may realize that there's a difference between northern and southern Presbyterians on this. Back as far back as 1756, the American Presbyterian General Assembly allowed for a separate body of men, people, to be appointed called trustees who would take care of the money and the property and take that off of the deacons so that they could be more concerned with helping people in need. The trouble is that trustees very often, though they're not ordained and though everybody can say, well, these people do not have the authority of the elders, it does sometimes create an organizational nightmare of three different bodies of people that you have to, three different boards that you've got to get approval of to do anything. And so, because some folks really had a great deal of trouble having a set of officers that the Bible never really defines anywhere, that James Henley Thornwell felt so strongly about that when the Southern Presbyterian Church broke away during the Civil War, the Southern Presbyterians say, forget the trustees. We will never have trustees. And so all the duties of trusteeship have always been given to the deacons. Northern churches have had more of a tendency to go the way of having trustees. And so the southern Presbyterian churches, there is the least consciousness amongst deacons, or amongst churches, of deacons being ministers of mercy for that very reason. Because this is the main thing that they do. Now, I think that they're right. I think that all three of these functions are valid. You see, the reason mercy has got to be given priority is for two reasons, maybe even three. Number one, Acts 6, though it's true that the seven were not deacons, they very, very clearly were the prototype for the act of ministry. We know, for example, that the early Roman church, by the end of the first century, the Roman church had 141 elders and only seven deacons. You know why? Because they said, well, it's just what the Bible says. You should only have seven. Which, of course, is rather poor exegesis. But the point was, it's very clear that all the early deacons based their ministry on what the seven were doing. And we also know that the meaning of the word diakonia, from which the word diakonos comes, the meaning of the word, its most basic meaning is to feed somebody. It's to wait on a table. And you can see it being used again and again and again in the Bible. So if the word basically means to feed, and the ministry of the seven was obviously the prototype, we have a lot of evidence for this being the primary purpose of the deacon, so these also could enter in. I've got a question about that. I'd like to see us say this is the primary purpose. We must not let these things get in the way of this at all, but that all three of these are valid purposes for the deaconate. And I'm going to keep on going, of course, but in a minute the bell's going to ring, but you've probably got time for a comment if somebody wants to give a comment or ask a question here. Yeah, Bob? It doesn't seem like that's the emphasis. No. Oh, no. Well, you see, why is this very often the thing that just consumes the deacons? Part of it would be middle-class captivity. Yeah. Yeah. Well, let me just see. For example, Tom Courtney, a mission of the world PCA pastor in Mexico, when he was starting a church amongst the poor in the poor side of Acapulco, he went to the deacons in the middle class Presbyterian church they had planted in the middle class section of Acapulco. And he asked that those deacons would come along with him as he did evangelism amongst the poor. And the deacons from the middle class church were having a great time. They loved going along, sharing the gospel, finding out people's needs. What happened was, pretty soon the people in the middle class church started complaining and said, where are our deacons? Do you realize we have light bulbs that are burning out in here? And that nobody's keeping the rug clean. And we have got to have that. And they really raised a ruckus. What are the deacons doing traipsing all over the place? And they pulled them back in. And so there's a very clear case of this sort of thing, swallowing up this sort of thing, largely because of class captivity, you see. And also because of the problem of who do you give this to? I mean, that's a fair question, and that is if you don't have trustees, who gets the job? And if the deacons have it, you realize this sort of thing can gobble up other sorts of work. Got to cut it off. Stuart, if you have a question, come on up here.

For all other information, please visit the main website at www.wts.edu. The Achanal ministry and lay ministry, let me just remind you of a couple of these things.

diaconal ministry and lay ministry. There's a pretty interesting... I'm going to refer to this because I don't think I could possibly draw a pyramid again. What we've been talking about is the bottom part of this pyramid...

and we're also talking about the side, the priestly side of this pyramid. We've been talking about diaconal ministry, and we're also talking about lay ministry. I think that it's pretty interesting to keep in mind that the church... I'm talking about the evangelical church in general now, not just the Reformed church. The church in general...

has really not got a very good grip on the concept that every believer is a prophet, a priest, and a king. Frank Tillepaw, who has written a book, The Unleashing of the Church, though I think in one edition it's called The Church Unleashed, maybe the more modern edition or the later edition it's called Unleashing the Church, whatever,

He has a set of tapes that will be awfully intriguing for you to get. They're called The Church Unleashed. There's six tapes. You can get them from his church. They go a lot further than the book goes. And he, in there, tells a couple of reasons why the church as it is today is in a situation where there is a passive laity and where outreach to the world is also...

truncated. He talks about the making of a fortress church. A fortress church to him means a church that stays in, does not reach out, and it also means a church in which the laity are passive. And he has a couple of pretty interesting principles, well not principles, a couple of explanations.

for why the church got to be the way it is and what to do about it. And I put these things down in terms of four statements. They're the sort of common sorts of statements you might hear people say. The first statement is, it's the they can come to us statement. Tillapa believes and says that part of the passive laity is because of the...

what he calls the parachurch explosion. Since World War II in this country, a terrific amount of outreach ministry has gone on through parachurch ministries. Now, by the way, Dilipat is not being negative about parachurch. Let me tell you what he says. He says he was a navigator, and I would never have been a navigator, so I may be not recounting his history as well as I should.

to Dawson Trotman, who was trying to reach young sailors, when he tried to get churches to reach out to the sailors in town, the typical response was, well, we have a singles group, or we have a college and career group. Let them come to us. And what Trotman decided was that if you're going to go to people, rather than say, let them come to us,

you're going to have to do an end run around the local church. Because the local church was stuck in a position where it said, we have our groups. We have our men's group and our women's group. We have our youth group and our college and career group and so on. If people want to, if you're going to reach people, let them come to us. Our doors are open to everybody. And Trotman decided, my word, if I'm going to really reach people, I'm going to have to do an end run around the church. So what he has done...

was he started the Navigators, which was a parachurch ministry, a specialized ministry that went out to the people who were sailors, the people who were in the military, went to them and found them and grabbed them and won them. Now, Telepah says when you ask the typical church, when you ask anybody, what does the church do? When you think of a local church, what does it do? You think of six or eight things. Think of worship.

and preaching. You think of the ministry of music. You think of Sunday school. You think of men's groups, women's groups, children's ministries, youth groups. But as Tillapa says, when you think of the church, you don't think of jail ministries. You don't think of ministries to unwed mothers. You don't think of ministries to the military. You don't think of ministries to international students. You don't think of all these kinds of ministries. Basically, if you're not white, upper-middle-class family, you don't think of all these kinds of ministries. Basically, if you're not white, upper-middle-class family,

There's not much place for you in the church. And almost anyone who has wanted to reach for Christ, any group in this country, besides a white upper middle class family group, has almost had to go do an end run around the evangelical church and form some kind of parent church ministry that actually reaches college students, or actually reaches high school dropouts, or who reaches prisoners, or who, you see what I'm saying.

They had to become parachurch ministries. The thing that's a little bit embarrassing is that though the parachurch ministries have always said we're an arm of the church, the parachurch ministries have become much more vital in many cases in the church, the local church. For example, and again, I know I'm being taped and so on, so I probably should have checked and double-checked all of my...

all of the statements, but Frank Tillepa says that the largest missionary sending body among denominations in the world is the Southern Baptist Church, but the Campus Crusade for Christ actually has three times the number of missionaries that the Southern Baptist Church has got. And that the parachurch ministries, by and large, are far more vital than local churches.

And it can be a little bit embarrassing in a sense because the parachurch ministry, the parachurch is saying we're an arm of the church, but if you consider the arm being this big and the rest of the body being this big, it does look a little bit strange. In a certain sense, parachurch ministries are the fishermen and the local church has decided we're the aquarium. And...

Now, who's to blame for that? There's a certain sense in which the parachurch ministries have developed because of this mentality, but the parachurch ministries, to a certain degree, because they've had to do an in-run around the local church, have continued to contribute to that mentality. If you want to reach prostitutes, form a parachurch ministry.

Why? I mean, you don't think any church is going to do that. The church won't be specialized enough. The church won't get behind it. You want to do that, you have to form your own ministry, a parachurch ministry, you see. So the let them come to us is a mentality that Telepost says that it has gone along with creating a fortress church.

And that is this bifurcation between parachurch, fishermen, and the local church, which continues to be kind of an aquarium. It's unfortunate, however, that an awful lot of the people that parachurch ministries reach just don't fit in most local churches. They don't fit. They're because very often they're not families or because they're not our kind of people. And very often parachurch ministries develop their own, almost become their own kind of church for that reason.

Another reason that Tilipa mentions that they're part of the making of the fortress church, we must have our needs met. Now, Tilipa calls this class captivity. Let me briefly explain what he says here. After World War II, again, we're talking about America, in this country,

We had a problem. America, in order to win World War II, had taken all of its vast resources, and we have a lot of resources here, and we had developed an incredible manufacturing capacity. In order to win the war, we were just producing planes and bombs and tanks and producing...

manufactured goods at a rate that the world had never seen before, that no country had ever been able to muster that kind of manufacturing capacity. Suddenly, as soon as we had no war, we had a problem. The whole economy was based on manufacturing, so we had to do something. And what actually happened was, in the late 40s and early 50s, we had a phenomenon called advertising.

The advertising industry convinced Americans that they needed an awful lot of goods in order to make us incredible consumers, the greatest consumers in the world, so that we could keep this incredible manufacturing machine alive and so that the economy could continue to progress. And they did it. There's no group of people in the world that believes that they need more goods than Americans.

And because American middle class people are so consumer oriented, above all, we love inventory. We like to pick and to choose. We're highly, highly, highly, highly aware of our needs. As a result, middle class churches have become commissaries. The churches is, this is Telepaw's idea. It uses that term, commissary.

that the evangelical church, by and large, is captive to the middle class and to the agenda of the middle class. What I mean by that is, number one, it means that the middle class says to the churches, if you meet our needs, if you have enough choirs and handbell choirs, if you have enough of an inventory, enough programs that meet our needs, we'll come to you.

And so the middle class church tends to orient itself toward issues of property. Middle class churches like to have nice carpeting and like to have a big wing and like to have a marble building and that sort of thing. Ministries assume that people have got the basic good quality of life. Middle class churches do not minister to people who don't have the basic safe life. They don't minister to non-middle class people.

Middle-class churches would rather spend money on property than people in general, rather than pour its money into people's needs. Middle-class churches would like to have a bigger sanctuary, would like to have bigger events, bigger worship services, bigger choirs, and so forth. But in general, the middle class says, if you meet our needs...

will come to you. And so churches, the evangelical church is more of a client, evangelical church people are more of a clientele than a congregation. That's what Martin Marty says. You understand the difference between a clientele and a congregation? It's very easy to grow a church as long as you study the market.

I'm using the term church growth in the most nasty way. It's very easy to swell your roles. If you segment the market and you figure out what the people in this particular area want, and then you program to meet those needs, you'll have people come. Because we're so incredibly consumer-oriented. That's the reason why, by and large, you find more of the super churches in this country than you do other places in the world in many cases.

Anyway, we must have our needs met. But that contributes to a fortress church, you see. The people come to get their needs met, not to pour themselves out, you see, in deeds of compassion and care and service to people around them. They come to have their needs being met. A third factor making for the fortress church, we can't work with you, is...

Well, it's the controversies. You have to realize that because of the great liberal fundamentalist controversy in the country, you have a great bifurcation between the fundamentalists who feel like they have to defend the faith and the liberals who in many cases have got...

a good social conscience. And one of the great difficulties we have is a big bifurcation between churches that put a lot of emphasis on teaching and emphasis on regeneration and churches that put emphasis on ministry and service to people. And frankly, in a church where the theology is universalistic and where the preaching cannot possibly create regenerate people...

And you need regenerate people with the power of the Spirit to really pour themselves out in deeds of ministry to people. Here you've got churches where the preaching can't produce power, where the people are being asked to do all kinds of tremendous programs pouring themselves out for people. And then here you've got churches that are just growing fat, on the other hand.

with people who are learning from the Word of God and people who are growing in grace. And very often, as they get older, they're growing in their pocketbooks. But all they do when they come together is talk. They talk about this stuff. They have seminars. They have classes. All they do is talk. And because of that bifurcation and because...

The way Frank Tillipoff puts it, because of all the liberal fundamentalist controversies, we're very, very suspicious of one another. And when it says we can't work with you, that refers to the kind of attitude that means if you don't toe the line, if you don't toe our doctrinal line, if you don't look like you're one of us.

We can't possibly work with you. It means, for example, that pastors and officers are scared to let lay people lead unless the lay people are as thoroughly schooled in the doctrine as they are. And basically what we're telling lay people is that until you become as well-schooled in doctrine as we are, we don't want you to really take initiative. We don't want you to reach out. We don't want you to minister. You wait for us to tell you what to do.

or you sign up on the bulletin board under the sheets where we have decided what ministries are to be done. And telepopulities, to a great degree, it's the denominational splits and the liberal fundamentalist controversy is a problem. Another area, where are your credentials? This refers to, and this is another factor in the making of Fortress Church, Passive Laity. I...

White evangelical churches, by and large, are awfully, awfully uptight about people having the degrees, having the right credentials for things. We have a Greek model of education. The Greek model of education is totally academic. It's very different than Jesus' model. See, the way in which Jesus taught his disciples was not that he had them come to a classroom.

where he lectured, but instead he picked the disciples up and he took them out into the world. And as things happened to them, Jesus would say, notice this, notice this, and he would teach as he went. He had an apprenticeship model. He had a life-on-a-life model, a discipling model. Now what's interesting is parachurch ministries, by and large, are very anti-seminary. Is that just an accident? Parachurch ministries are very vital in terms of outreach. Parachurch ministries are very anti-clerical.

They don't like to have a lot of ministers around. They're run by lay people. Why is that? I think because in some ways they're more in tune with Jesus' model of letting lay people minister, of training them on the job and making sure they're being trained in wisdom as well as knowledge.

You see, in a lot of ways, they are more in tune with what the Bible says about the fact that every believer is a prophet and a priest and a king. But in the fortress church, you have the attitude that really only the officers are prophets, priests, and kings. We can't trust the lay people. Or lay people are, because they're under the middle class American...

They don't think of themselves as prophets, priests, and kings. They want to find the best prophet and the best priest and the best kings in town so they can go and have their needs met. They don't think of themselves as prophets, priests, and kings. That's behind the fortress church. And I think that...

Boy, I think that what Tilapa is saying is something that is really, really important. He says what we have to do in order to overcome that is to press people that they are ministers, messengers, and managers, and that the lay people need to be told that, and that then they have to be shown that we do trust in the minister. One thing you might find kind of interesting is...

Telepah hates committees, absolutely hates committees. In fact, I don't think he has a committee in his church. He may overdo this, but he says when he was in the army, he said whenever you're on the front line of a war, you will find that on the front line where your life is on the line, there's a lot of camaraderie, there's a lot of...

cohesion to the team. The people are working with each other because, man, your life is on the line. We're buddies. We've got to work together. We've got to pull together. We've got to get the morale is often high, at least unless there's been a whole lot of horrible defeats. But you go back a couple of miles, just a couple of miles from the battle line, he would say, where you have the supply line.

and the supply camps, and there's nothing but complaining and grumbling and mumbling about the food and backbiting between parties and so forth. And he says the reason that most churches are in a position where they are like the supply line camps rather than the front line camps is because we keep most lay people in rear echelon ministries. We put them on Christian ed committees and we put them on music committees and we put them on all kinds of committees instead of saying to the lay people,

You should be in the jails. You should be on the college campuses. You should be in the ghetto. You should be out there ministering to people. That's front line kinds of ministry. And so he says, for example, instead of having a Christian ed committee that runs the Vacation Bible School as well as Sunday School, instead you should be saying, okay, lay people, is there anybody out there that's got a burden for ministry to children? Get together and do it.

If there's nobody with a burden for a vacation Bible school this year, if there's nobody that wants to do it, nobody's got a burden on their heart to do it, we're not going to do it. If you have a Christian education committee, you've institutionalized vacation Bible school. By institutionalizing, I mean you appoint people to this Christian education committee. The person gets on there, maybe they don't even really want to get on there, but they get on there because you've pulled their leg. And they say, okay, what does the Christian education committee do? One of the things is we run vacation Bible school. Who's going to be the director this year?

Well, I don't know, we're going to have to go find one. And you get up there and say, we won't even be able to have to have a Christian education, we won't be able to have a vacation Bible school this year unless somebody volunteers as a director. So you work on the congregation to get, you know, using guilt and so on. And a committee structure, Telepas says, institutionalizes and creates a rear echelon mentality. What lies behind that?

those factors that we just went over. Instead, tell lay people, we are letting you minister here. We want you to minister here. You see a need, come to us and say, I want to meet that need. Get together the other people who want to meet that need. Go to it. We'll guide you, we'll help you, we'll support you. We're not going to control you. We're not necessarily going to look at your doctrine up and down before we let you even make a move.

So, telepath says, this is what you have to do. You have to go about really making sure that we break out of the fortress church. Now, as far as I understand, the Reformed ecclesiology has got the theology, at least, to break out of the fortress church mentality. I mean, even telepath's book, as good as it is, doesn't have the power of being able to say, every believer is a king.

That's why we can break out of the fortress church. He doesn't have the theology. That's powerful theology. He doesn't have the theology behind it. But he has a general sense of what the scripture says about the ministry of the lady and does a good job in that book. But Reformed Ecclesiology has got dynamite in there for lay people. Dynamite. But what has kept us from exploding?

What's kept us from exploding? Things like this. Middle class mentality. To a certain degree, the problem of the parachurch, I'm not trying to blame the church or the parachurch, but I'm trying to say something's got to be done here. We sure shouldn't be living in two different worlds like this. One of the problems with being reformed is that we have a much clearer understanding of what is accurate, the doctrine, than anybody else in the world. You see? And...

these factors have, to a certain degree, put water on our gunpowder. But there's a tremendous amount of gunpowder in this theology. We should be exploding, but we're not. Now, let me stop there and see whether or not somebody wants to say something. Bob? I would guess that there may be some tension between the fear and trembling aspects of...

I think I understand what you're saying. On the one hand... The unqualified Sunday school teachers. Yeah, well you see, some people in here have told me, some people here in school have told me one of the great dangers about...

about getting all this theology at Westminster Seminary, is some people told me that they feel somewhat paralyzed in ministry, because they said, back when I was ignorant, back when I didn't know there was so much truth, back when I didn't know there was so much falsehood, back when I thought there might be five or six heresies, I didn't realize there's at least five million.

I was more loosey-goosey. I, in some ways, was more ready to get up and try to exhort people and ready to lead a group of people out into the world and so on. And now I'm scared. And I think that's what you're kind of talking about. And not only that, it makes us scared about other people. We look at other people and they say, I'm ready to teach a class.

And if you know all this material, you sit there and say, oh, you poor, ignorant person. You don't realize how many errors you could fall into just by opening your mouth. My suggestion is that you can't, whatever the balance is between healthy fear and trembling, wanting not to...

misuse the Word of God, rightly divide the Word of God, and also see what the Bible says about believers. You know, like in Acts 8.4, D. James Kennedy's like verse, that after this persecution, in Acts 8, the persecution of Stephen, Stephen's being killed and so on, it says everyone was scattered except the apostles. You know that verse? The apostles stayed in Jerusalem, everyone else was scattered, and it says they went everywhere preaching the Word. Use the word preach. Everybody went preaching the Word.

That's James, you know, that's Kennedy's life verse. And when you see all the things the Bible says that lay people can do, everybody can preach, everybody can counsel. That's Jay Adams' whole approach. Every Christian can counsel. When you see all the places the Bible says we should be exhorting one another, confessing sins to one another, bearing one another's burdens, and so on, we've got to make sure that that healthy sense of fear and trembling doesn't paralyze us, because then we know we're disobedient if we're doing nothing.
